title: Ὄνειρος οὖλος
about: While gods and men sleep, Zeus lies awake, working out how to honour Achilles by making the Achaeans suffer. He sends a ruinous Dream to Agamemnon, in the shape of Nestor, with a message that Troy can be taken at once, since Hera has won over the gods. Agamemnon wakes believing it, dresses, and goes along the ships as Dawn climbs Olympus; heralds summon the army, and he first gathers the elders by Nestor's ship. He tells them the dream, then proposes to test the army by telling it to flee, with the elders ready to hold it back. Nestor rises and says that, had anyone else told such a dream, they would reject it, but as the man who claims to be the best has seen it, they should try to arm the army.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι μέν ῥα θεοί τε καὶ ἀνέρες ἱπποκορυσταὶ
εὗδον παννύχιοι, Δία δ’ οὐκ ἔχε νήδυμος ὕπνος,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε μερμήριζε κατὰ φρένα ὡς Ἀχιλῆα
τιμήσῃ, ὀλέσῃ δὲ πολέας ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
Other gods, indeed, and horse-arming men
slept all night long, but Zeus sweet sleep did not hold,
but he kept pondering in his mind how Achilles
he should honour, and destroy many beside the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: All the other gods, and the men armed with horses, slept the whole night through, but sweet sleep did not hold Zeus; he kept pondering in his mind how he might honour Achilles and destroy many men beside the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἱπποκορυσταί joins ἵππος ‘horse’ to κορύσσω ‘arm, equip’ (from κόρυς ‘helmet’). ‘Armed with horses’ is the literal form; whether it meant chariot-fighters or men with horsehair-crested helmets is not known. νήδυμος ὕπνος: the meaning of νήδυμος is not known, and ‘sweet’ is only the traditional guess. Δία is the accusative: all sleep, but sleep did not hold Zeus. μερμήριζε is an imperfect, ‘kept pondering’, with ὡς ‘how’ and the subjunctives τιμήσῃ, ὀλέσῃ for what he might do. The aim is the favour to Achilles that Thetis asked of Zeus, and he promised, in the last two parts.

sentences.t:
ἥδε δέ οἱ κατὰ θυμὸν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλή,
πέμψαι ἐπ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι οὖλον ὄνειρον·
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.i: And this seemed to him in his heart the best plan: to send a ruinous Dream to Agamemnon, son of Atreus. And lifting his voice he spoke winged words to the Dream:
sentences.n: ἥδε ‘this’ points forward to the infinitive πέμψαι: the plan that seemed best was to send a Dream. οἱ is the dative ‘to him’, and Ἀτρεΐδῃ is the dative of Ἀτρεΐδης, ‘son of Atreus’. Ὄνειρος ‘Dream’ is a being Zeus can send and speak to (the vocative follows). οὖλον ‘ruinous’ is from the root of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’, as in οὐλομένην (1.2). Line 7 is the line of 1.201, where μιν was Athena; here it is the Dream, so ‘to it’ and ‘to the Dream’ replace ‘to her’. Two sentences are joined here, because the second is only the speech-introduction.

sentences.t: βάσκ’ ἴθι οὖλε ὄνειρε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: “Go, set out, ruinous Dream, to the swift ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: “Be off with you, ruinous Dream, to the swift ships of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: βάσκ’ ἴθι is a pair of imperatives, from βάσκω (a lengthened form of βαίνω) and εἶμι, ‘be off, go’. οὖλε ὄνειρε is a vocative: Zeus speaks to the Dream by name. This οὖλος ‘ruinous’ (cf. ὄλλυμι) is not the unrelated οὖλος ‘whole’. θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν is the stock phrase; θοός ‘swift’ is translated each time, and ἐπί with the accusative marks the goal.

sentences.t:
ἐλθὼν ἐς κλισίην Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο
πάντα μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορευέμεν ὡς ἐπιτέλλω·
sentences.l:
having come to the hut of Agamemnon, Atreus’-son,
everything, very exactly, to declare as I enjoin;
sentences.i: go to the hut of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, and declare everything to him, very exactly, as I charge you;
sentences.n: ἐλθών ‘having come’ hangs on the command in ἀγορευέμεν, an infinitive used as an imperative (‘declare!’), which Homer often does. κλισίη, built on κλίνω ‘lean’, is the hut or shelter a leader lives in at the camp. Ἀτρεΐδαο has the epic genitive in -αο (= Attic -ου). ὡς ἐπιτέλλω ‘as I enjoin’ uses the verb of 1.25 (ἐπὶ … ἔτελλε, ‘laid a charge on’).

sentences.t:
θωρῆξαί ἑ κέλευε κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιοὺς
πανσυδίῃ·
sentences.l:
to arm, bid him, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
with-all-rush;
sentences.i: bid him arm the long-haired Achaeans with all speed;
sentences.n: θωρῆξαι ‘to arm’ is from θωρήσσω (θώραξ ‘breastplate’); κέλευε is the imperative ‘bid’, and ἑ ‘him’ (Agamemnon) is the subject of the infinitive. κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς: κάρη is an accusative of respect (‘long-haired as to the head’) and κομόωντας the uncontracted participle (Attic κομῶντας); the epithet is translated each time. πανσυδίῃ is πᾶς + σεύομαι ‘rush’; its exact sense is uncertain, ‘with all speed’ or ‘in full force’.

sentences.t:
νῦν γάρ κεν ἕλοι πόλιν εὐρυάγυιαν
Τρώων·
sentences.l:
for now he might take the wide-streeted city
of the Trojans;
sentences.i: for now he could take the Trojans’ city of the wide streets;
sentences.n: νῦν γάρ ‘for now’ gives the reason: the moment has come. κεν with the optative ἕλοι (αἱρέω ‘take’) makes a possibility, ‘he could take’. εὐρυάγυιαν ‘with wide streets’ (εὐρύς + ἀγυιά ‘street’) is an epithet of cities, here of Troy. Τρώων begins line 13 and belongs with πόλιν.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἀμφὶς Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες
ἀθάνατοι φράζονται·
sentences.l:
for no longer apart, who hold the Olympian halls,
the immortals plan;
sentences.i: for the immortals who hold the halls of Olympus no longer plan apart from one another;
sentences.n: ἀμφίς ‘apart, divided’: the gods who quarrelled in the last part now plan as one, as the message says. Ὀλύμπια is a neuter plural adjective with δώματα, and ἔχοντες ‘holding’ gives the stock phrase for the gods, who hold the halls of Olympus. φράζονται is the middle of φράζω, ‘plan, take thought’. These two lines come three times in this part: here, in the Dream’s words (30–31) and in Agamemnon’s retelling (67–68), always with the same English.

sentences.t:
ἐπέγναμψεν γὰρ ἅπαντας
Ἥρη λισσομένη, Τρώεσσι δὲ κήδε’ ἐφῆπται.
sentences.l:
for she has bent them all,
Hera, entreating, and on the Trojans sorrows are fastened.”
sentences.i: for Hera, entreating them, has swayed them all, and sorrows have been fastened upon the Trojans.”
sentences.n: ἐπέγναμψεν is the aorist of ἐπιγνάμπτω ‘bend’, here ‘bend to one’s will’, and ἅπαντας ‘all’ is the whole company of the gods. Ἥρη has Ionic η, λισσομένη is ‘entreating’ (λίσσομαι), and κήδε’ is κήδεα ‘sorrows’ with the vowel elided. ἐφῆπται, the perfect passive of ἐφάπτω, is ‘have been fastened on’. Lines 37–40 show that the news is a lure: the hope it raises will fail.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, βῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὄνειρος ἐπεὶ τὸν μῦθον ἄκουσε·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the Dream went, when it had heard the word;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Dream went on its way when it had heard the word;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the usual close to a speech; φάτο is the unaugmented (ἔφατο) form of φημί. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist ἔβη ‘went’, ἄρ’ marks the sequel, and ἄκουσε is ἤκουσε without the augment. τὸν μῦθον ‘the word’ has the article in its older pointing force, ‘that word’. The edition begins a new paragraph at this line.

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως δ’ ἵκανε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν,
βῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα·
sentences.l:
Swiftly he reached the swift ships of the Achaeans,
and went to Atreus’-son Agamemnon;
sentences.i: Swiftly he came to the swift ships of the Achaeans and went to Agamemnon, son of Atreus;
sentences.n: καρπαλίμως is an adverb, ‘swiftly’. ἵκανε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’. θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν repeats the end of Zeus’s first command (line 8), the journey done in the same words. βῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ takes the accusative: ‘went to’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ κίχανεν
εὕδοντ’ ἐν κλισίῃ, περὶ δ’ ἀμβρόσιος κέχυθ’ ὕπνος.
sentences.l:
and him he found
sleeping in the hut, and about him ambrosial sleep was poured.
sentences.i: and found him asleep in his hut, with ambrosial sleep poured about him.
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ κίχανεν: τόν is ‘him’ (Agamemnon), and κίχανεν is the unaugmented imperfect of κιχάνω ‘find, come upon’. εὕδοντ’ is the participle εὕδοντα ‘sleeping’. κέχυθ’ is κέχυτο, the pluperfect passive of χέω ‘pour’: the sleep had been poured around him like a liquid. ἀμβρόσιος ‘ambrosial’ (from ἄμβροτος ‘deathless’) says the sleep is of the gods’ kind; it recurs in ἀμβροσίην … νύκτα (57).

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς Νηληΐῳ υἷι ἐοικώς
Νέστορι, τόν ῥα μάλιστα γερόντων τῖ’ Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.l:
And he stood above his head, to Neleus’ son likened,
Nestor, whom most of the elders Agamemnon honoured;
sentences.i: He stood above his head in the likeness of Nestor, son of Neleus, the one of all the elders whom Agamemnon honoured most;
sentences.n: στῆ is the unaugmented ἔστη ‘stood’; ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς with the genitive is ‘above his head’, where dream-figures stand over a sleeper. ἐοικώς, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, ‘being like’, takes the dative; Νηληΐῳ is an adjective, ‘of Neleus’, so Νηληΐῳ υἷι … Νέστορι is ‘to the Neleian son, Nestor’. τῖ’ is τῖε, the unaugmented imperfect of τίω ‘honour’, and γερόντων is a partitive genitive: the one among the elders. The Dream takes the shape of the man Agamemnon honours most.

sentences.t: τῷ μιν ἐεισάμενος προσεφώνεε θεῖος ὄνειρος·
sentences.l: Having made himself like to him, spoke to him the divine Dream:
sentences.i: Making himself like Nestor, the divine Dream spoke to him:
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘to him’ (Nestor), governed by ἐεισάμενος, the aorist middle participle of εἴδομαι ‘make oneself seem like’; μιν is Agamemnon, the object of προσεφώνεε, the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. θεῖος ‘divine’ (from θεός) says the Dream is of the god’s sending; it is kept apart from δῖος ‘heavenly’. The colon opens the Dream’s speech, which Agamemnon will repeat almost word for word at 60–70.

sentences.t: εὕδεις Ἀτρέος υἱὲ δαΐφρονος ἱπποδάμοιο·
sentences.l: “You sleep, son of Atreus, wise-minded, horse-taming;
sentences.i: “You are sleeping, son of wise-hearted Atreus, tamer of horses;
sentences.n: εὕδεις ‘you sleep’ is a reproach. Ἀτρέος υἱέ is a vocative, ‘son of Atreus’, and the epithets δαΐφρονος and ἱπποδάμοιο (epic genitive in -οιο) belong to Atreus. δαΐφρων is uncertain in sense, from δαῆναι ‘learn’ (‘wise’) or from δαΐ ‘in battle’ (‘warlike’), and ‘wise-minded’ follows the first reading. ἱπποδάμοιο is ἵππος ‘horse’ + δάμνημι ‘tame’.

sentences.t:
οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα
ᾧ λαοί τ’ ἐπιτετράφαται καὶ τόσσα μέμηλε·
sentences.l:
it is not right all night to sleep, a man who bears counsel,
to whom peoples have been entrusted and so many things are a care;
sentences.i: A man who bears counsel must not sleep the whole night through, a man to whom the people are entrusted and who has so many cares;
sentences.n: οὐ χρή ‘it is not right, one must not’ takes the infinitive εὕδειν. παννύχιον is an adjective used as an adverb, ‘all night’. βουληφόρον ἄνδρα is ‘a man who bears counsel’ (βουλή ‘counsel’ + φέρω ‘bear’). ᾧ ‘to whom’; ἐπιτετράφαται is the perfect passive of ἐπιτρέπω ‘entrust’ with the epic ending -αται (Attic -νται), and μέμηλε the perfect of μέλω ‘be a care’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἐμέθεν ξύνες ὦκα·
sentences.l: But now, to me give heed quickly;
sentences.i: But now listen to me, and quickly;
sentences.n: ξύνες is the aorist imperative of συνίημι ‘take in, give heed to’, with the old spelling ξυν- (as in ξυνέηκε, 1.8), and ἐμέθεν is the epic genitive of ἐγώ. ὦκα is the adverb ‘quickly’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, as do the same words in Agamemnon’s retelling (63).

sentences.t:
Διὸς δέ τοι ἄγγελός εἰμι,
ὃς σεῦ ἄνευθεν ἐὼν μέγα κήδεται ἠδ’ ἐλεαίρει.
sentences.l:
but of Zeus, to you, a messenger I am,
who, though far from you, greatly cares for and pities you.
sentences.i: I am a messenger of Zeus to you, who, though he is far from you, cares greatly for you and pities you.
sentences.n: Διὸς … ἄγγελος ‘messenger of Zeus’: the Dream names its sender. τοι here is the dative σοι ‘to you’ (it could also be the particle τοι, ‘mark you’). σεῦ ἄνευθεν ἐών is the epic genitive σεῦ with ἄνευθεν ‘far from’ and the participle ἐών (Attic ὤν); κήδεται and ἐλεαίρει have no object of their own written, and ‘you’ is understood for both from σεῦ. ἐλεαίρω ‘pity’ is the epic by-form of ἐλεέω.

sentences.t:
θωρῆξαί σε κέλευσε κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιοὺς
πανσυδίῃ·
sentences.l:
to arm, he has bidden you, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
with-all-rush;
sentences.i: he has bidden you arm the long-haired Achaeans with all speed;
sentences.n: This repeats lines 11–12, with σε ‘you’ for ἑ ‘him’: Zeus gave the order in the third person, the Dream gives it in the second. κέλευσε is the aorist, ‘he has bidden’. Nothing else changes but the verb form, and the English repeats.

sentences.t:
νῦν γάρ κεν ἕλοις πόλιν εὐρυάγυιαν
Τρώων·
sentences.l:
for now you might take the wide-streeted city
of the Trojans;
sentences.i: for now you could take the Trojans’ city of the wide streets;
sentences.n: ἕλοις is the second-person optative of αἱρέω ‘take’, where line 12 had ἕλοι ‘he might take’. The rest is as in 12–13.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἀμφὶς Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες
ἀθάνατοι φράζονται·
sentences.l:
for no longer apart, who hold the Olympian halls,
the immortals plan;
sentences.i: for the immortals who hold the halls of Olympus no longer plan apart from one another;
sentences.n: The gods’ agreement is repeated word for word, as in lines 13–14; the Dream gives the reason Zeus gave. See the first occurrence for the forms.

sentences.t:
ἐπέγναμψεν γὰρ ἅπαντας
Ἥρη λισσομένη, Τρώεσσι δὲ κήδε’ ἐφῆπται
ἐκ Διός·
sentences.i: for Hera, entreating them, has swayed them all, and sorrows have been fastened upon the Trojans from Zeus;
sentences.n: These words repeat lines 14–15, with one addition: ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’ (ἐκ with the genitive of source), which line 15 did not have, since there Zeus himself was speaking. Here the Dream names the source of the Trojans’ sorrows. This is the Dream’s own wording, not Zeus’s, and the speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ σῇσιν ἔχε φρεσί, μηδέ σε λήθη
αἱρείτω εὖτ’ ἄν σε μελίφρων ὕπνος ἀνήῃ.
sentences.l:
but you, in your own wits hold it, and let not forgetfulness
seize you, when honey-hearted sleep lets you go.”
sentences.i: but keep this in your own mind, and do not let forgetfulness seize you when heart-sweetening sleep lets you go.”
sentences.n: σῇσιν is the epic dative plural of σός ‘your own’ (not a relative), with φρεσί, the dative plural of φρήν ‘wits’; ἔχε is ‘hold it, keep it’. μηδέ σε λήθη αἱρείτω is a third-person imperative, ‘let forgetfulness not seize you’; εὖτ’ ἄν … ἀνήῃ is ‘when … lets go’ (ἀνίημι, with the subjunctive). μελίφρων is μέλι ‘honey’ + φρήν; its sense is uncertain, and ‘heart-sweetening’ follows the Odyssey’s ‘heart-sweetening wine’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπεβήσετο, τὸν δὲ λίπ’ αὐτοῦ
τὰ φρονέοντ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ἅ ῥ’ οὐ τελέεσθαι ἔμελλον·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, he went away, and left him there
reckoning in his heart on things that were not going to be fulfilled;
sentences.i: With these words he went away and left him there, reckoning in his heart on things that were not to be fulfilled;
sentences.n: ἀπεβήσετο is the aorist middle of ἀποβαίνω with the epic ending -σετο, ‘went away’. τὸν δὲ λίπ’ αὐτοῦ: λίπ’ is the unaugmented λίπε ‘left’, τόν is Agamemnon, and αὐτοῦ ‘on the spot, there’. φρονέοντ’ is the participle ‘thinking, reckoning’ (uncontracted, Attic φρονοῦντα); τὰ … ἅ ‘those things which’; ἔμελλον τελέεσθαι ‘were going to be fulfilled’, the passive infinitive of τελέω. The narrator tells us at once that the hope is false.

sentences.t:
φῆ γὰρ ὅ γ’ αἱρήσειν Πριάμου πόλιν ἤματι κείνῳ
νήπιος, οὐδὲ τὰ ᾔδη ἅ ῥα Ζεὺς μήδετο ἔργα·
sentences.l:
for he thought he would take Priam’s city on that day,
foolish, and he did not know what deeds Zeus was devising;
sentences.i: For he thought he would take Priam’s city that very day, foolish as he was, and he did not know what deeds Zeus was devising;
sentences.n: φῆ is the unaugmented ἔφη, here ‘thought, said to himself’; αἱρήσειν is the future infinitive of αἱρέω ‘take’, and κείνῳ is the Ionic form of ἐκείνῳ ‘that’. νήπιος ‘foolish’ is the narrator’s comment, set after its sentence. ᾔδη is the past of οἶδα ‘knew’; τὰ … ἅ ‘the deeds that’; μήδετο is the unaugmented imperfect of μήδομαι ‘devise’.

sentences.t:
θήσειν γὰρ ἔτ’ ἔμελλεν ἐπ’ ἄλγεά τε στοναχάς τε
Τρωσί τε καὶ Δαναοῖσι διὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας.
sentences.l:
for he was yet to lay both pains and groans
on both Trojans and Danaans through strong battles.
sentences.i: For Zeus was still to lay pains and groans on Trojans and Danaans alike, through strong battles.
sentences.n: θήσειν γὰρ ἔτ’ ἔμελλεν: the subject is still Zeus, μέλλω ‘be going to’ takes the future infinitive of τίθημι, and ἐπί, which stands apart from it (tmesis), makes ‘lay upon’. ἄλγεα τε στοναχάς τε is ‘both pains and groans’. Τρωσί τε καὶ Δαναοῖσι is ‘on both Trojans and Danaans’; Δαναοί is one of the poet’s three names for the army. διά with the accusative is ‘through’; κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας ‘strong battles’.

sentences.t: ἔγρετο δ’ ἐξ ὕπνου, θείη δέ μιν ἀμφέχυτ’ ὀμφή·
sentences.l: And he woke from sleep, and the divine voice was poured about him;
sentences.i: He woke from sleep with the divine voice still poured about him;
sentences.n: ἔγρετο is the epic aorist middle of ἐγείρω, ‘woke’. θείη is the epic feminine of θεῖος ‘divine’, and ὀμφή is a voice with divine force behind it, a god’s utterance. ἀμφέχυτ’ is ἀμφέχυτο, the pluperfect passive of ἀμφιχέω ‘pour round’: the picture repeats the sleep poured round him at 19, now with the voice in its place. μιν ‘him’.

sentences.t:
ἕζετο δ’ ὀρθωθείς, μαλακὸν δ’ ἔνδυνε χιτῶνα
καλὸν νηγάτεον, περὶ δὲ μέγα βάλλετο φᾶρος·
sentences.l:
And he sat up, having been set upright, and put on a soft tunic,
fine, new-made, and about him threw a great cloak;
sentences.i: He sat up, put on a soft tunic, fine and newly made, and threw a great cloak about him;
sentences.n: ἕζετο ‘sat’ with ὀρθωθείς, the aorist passive participle of ὀρθόω ‘set upright’, is ‘sat up’. ἔνδυνε is the imperfect of ἐνδύνω ‘put on’; the χιτών is the tunic worn next to the skin, and the φᾶρος a large cloth worn over it as a cloak. νηγάτεον is a rare word glossed as ‘newly made’; its formation is not known. βάλλετο is the middle, ‘threw about himself’.

sentences.t:
ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ὤμοισιν βάλετο ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον·
sentences.l:
and under his sleek feet he bound fine sandals,
and about his shoulders he slung the silver-studded sword;
sentences.i: he bound fine sandals beneath his sleek feet and slung the silver-studded sword about his shoulders;
sentences.n: ποσσὶ … ὑπό: the preposition stands apart from its verb (tmesis), ‘bound under’. ποσσί is the epic dative of πούς, λιπαροῖσιν ‘sleek’ (shining with oil), and ἐδήσατο the aorist middle of δέω ‘bind’. The first line is a formula for dressing; the Odyssey has it too. ἀμφὶ … βάλετο is another tmesis, ‘slung about’; ἀργυρόηλον ‘silver-studded’ (ἀργυρός + ἧλος ‘nail, stud’).

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δὲ σκῆπτρον πατρώϊον ἄφθιτον αἰεὶ
σὺν τῷ ἔβη κατὰ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων·
sentences.l:
and he took up the sceptre of his fathers, unfailing for ever,
and with it went along the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans;
sentences.i: He took up his fathers’ sceptre, which never fails, and with it went along the ships of the bronze-shirted Achaeans;
sentences.n: εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω, ‘took up’. σκῆπτρον πατρώϊον is the sceptre handed down from his fathers, the sign of a king’s right to speak. ἄφθιτον ‘unfailing’ is ἀ- + φθίνω ‘waste away’, and αἰεί ‘for ever’. σὺν τῷ ‘with it’ uses τῷ as a pronoun. κατὰ νῆας is ‘along the ships’, and χαλκοχιτώνων ‘of the bronze-shirted’ (χαλκός + χιτών) is the stock epithet of the Achaeans, translated each time.

sentences.t:
ἠὼς μέν ῥα θεὰ προσεβήσετο μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον
Ζηνὶ φόως ἐρέουσα καὶ ἄλλοις ἀθανάτοισιν·
sentences.l:
Dawn, indeed, the goddess, went up to tall Olympus,
to Zeus light to announce and to the other immortals;
sentences.i: Dawn, the goddess, went up to tall Olympus to announce the light to Zeus and to the other immortals;
sentences.n: ἠώς is Dawn (Attic ἕως). μέν ῥα turns the story to a new scene while Agamemnon walks the camp. προσεβήσετο has the epic ending -σετο, as ἀπεβήσετο at 35, and takes the accusative of the goal, μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον ‘tall Olympus’. Ζηνί is the epic dative of Ζεύς. ἐρέουσα is a future participle, ‘about to say’, so ‘to announce’; its exact sense is uncertain.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ κηρύκεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισι κέλευσε
κηρύσσειν ἀγορὴν δὲ κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l:
But he to the clear-voiced heralds gave-command
to summon to assembly the long-haired-of-head Achaeans;
sentences.i: But he ordered the clear-voiced heralds to summon the long-haired Achaeans to assembly;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ and ὃ ‘he’ (Agamemnon). κηρύκεσσι is the epic dative plural of κῆρυξ ‘herald’. λιγυφθόγγοισι ‘clear-voiced’ is λιγύς ‘clear’ + φθόγγος ‘voice’, the heralds’ stock epithet. κέλευσε takes the dative and the infinitive: ‘ordered the heralds to summon’. ἀγορὴν δέ is ἀγορήνδε ‘to assembly’, with the direction suffix -δε; the edition prints it as two words.

sentences.t: οἳ μὲν ἐκήρυσσον, τοὶ δ’ ἠγείροντο μάλ’ ὦκα·
sentences.l: They made-proclamation, and the others gathered very quickly;
sentences.i: The heralds made the proclamation, and the people gathered very quickly;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν … τοὶ δ’ ‘these … those’, with the article used as a pronoun: the heralds and the people. ἐκήρυσσον is the imperfect, ‘kept proclaiming’, and ἠγείροντο the imperfect passive of ἐγείρω, ‘were roused, gathered’. μάλ’ ὦκα ‘very quickly’ matches ὦκα at 26 and 63.

sentences.t:
βουλὴν δὲ πρῶτον μεγαθύμων ἷζε γερόντων
Νεστορέῃ παρὰ νηῒ Πυλοιγενέος βασιλῆος·
sentences.l:
And a council first of the great-hearted elders he seated
beside the ship of Nestor, the Pylos-born king;
sentences.i: First he seated a council of the great-hearted elders beside the ship of Nestor, the king born at Pylos;
sentences.n: ἷζε is the transitive ‘made sit’ (ἵζω), so Agamemnon seats the council. βουλήν is concrete here, ‘a council’. μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’ is a stock epithet, and γερόντων ‘elders’. Νεστορέῃ is an adjective in the dative, ‘Nestor’s’, with νηῒ ‘ship’ (the diaeresis is printed). Πυλοιγενέος is Πύλος + -γενής ‘born’, and βασιλῆος the epic genitive of βασιλεύς, ‘king’.

sentences.t: τοὺς ὅ γε συγκαλέσας πυκινὴν ἀρτύνετο βουλήν·
sentences.l: These, having called them together, he arranged a close-packed plan:
sentences.i: He called them together and set out a shrewd plan:
sentences.n: τοὺς ὅ γε: ὅ γε ‘he’ is Agamemnon. συγκαλέσας is the aorist participle ‘having called together’. πυκινός ‘close-packed’ is used of counsel in the sense of ‘dense, shrewd’; βουλή is now ‘plan’, not the body in line 53. ἀρτύνετο is the imperfect middle of ἀρτύνω, ‘arranged, put in order’.

sentences.t: κλῦτε φίλοι·
sentences.l: “Hear, friends:
sentences.i: “Hear me, friends:
sentences.n: κλῦτε is the plural imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and φίλοι ‘friends’ the vocative. From here to line 71 Agamemnon retells the Dream: lines 60–69 repeat 23–32 almost word for word, and 70 stops short of the Dream’s warning at 33–34. Repeated words are given the same English each time.

sentences.t:
θεῖός μοι ἐνύπνιον ἦλθεν ὄνειρος
ἀμβροσίην διὰ νύκτα·
sentences.l:
a divine Dream came to me in sleep
through the ambrosial night;
sentences.i: A divine Dream came to me in my sleep through the ambrosial night;
sentences.n: θεῖός μοι ἐνύπνιον ἦλθεν ὄνειρος: ἐνύπνιον is the neuter adjective ‘in sleep’ used as an adverb, and μοι is ‘to me’. ἀμβροσίην διὰ νύκτα is ‘through the ambrosial night’ (διά with the accusative); like the sleep of line 19, the night is called ambrosial, of the gods’ kind. Agamemnon says plainly that the Dream was a god-sent one.

sentences.t:
μάλιστα δὲ Νέστορι δίῳ
εἶδός τε μέγεθός τε φυήν τ’ ἄγχιστα ἐῴκει·
sentences.l:
and most of all to Nestor, heavenly,
in form and in size and in stature it most nearly resembled;
sentences.i: and above all it resembled heavenly Nestor, most nearly in form, in size and in stature;
sentences.n: μάλιστα … ἄγχιστα: ‘most of all’ and ‘most nearly’. ἐῴκει is the pluperfect of ἔοικα, ‘resembled’, with the dative Νέστορι δίῳ. εἶδος, μέγεθος and φυή are accusatives of respect: ‘in form, in size and in stature’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet. Agamemnon’s words echo the description at 20–21.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς καί με πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
εὕδεις Ἀτρέος υἱὲ δαΐφρονος ἱπποδάμοιο·
sentences.l:
It stood above my head and spoke a word to me:
‘You sleep, son of Atreus, wise-minded, horse-taming;
sentences.i: It stood above my head and spoke to me: ‘You are sleeping, son of wise-hearted Atreus, tamer of horses;
sentences.n: στῆ … ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς repeats line 20. ἔειπεν is the epic form of εἶπεν ‘spoke’, and πρός goes with it (‘spoke to’), with μῦθον as its object. The Dream’s speech is a speech inside Agamemnon’s, so it takes single quotation marks, and its first line is that of 23. The two lines are one unit here so that the nested quotation can open without changing the repeated line.
sentences.mark: The Dream speaks, as Agamemnon tells it

sentences.t:
οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα,
ᾧ λαοί τ’ ἐπιτετράφαται καὶ τόσσα μέμηλε·
sentences.l:
it is not right all night to sleep, a man who bears counsel,
to whom peoples have been entrusted and so many things are a care;
sentences.i: A man who bears counsel must not sleep the whole night through, a man to whom the people are entrusted and who has so many cares;
sentences.n: These two lines repeat 24–25, with only a comma after ἄνδρα that line 24 lacks. See the first occurrence for οὐ χρή, βουληφόρον, ἐπιτετράφαται and μέμηλε.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἐμέθεν ξύνες ὦκα·
sentences.l: But now, to me give heed quickly;
sentences.i: But now listen to me, and quickly;
sentences.n: Word for word as line 26: ξύνες ὦκα ‘give heed quickly’.

sentences.t:
Διὸς δέ τοι ἄγγελός εἰμι,
ὃς σεῦ ἄνευθεν ἐὼν μέγα κήδεται ἠδ’ ἐλεαίρει·
sentences.l:
but of Zeus, to you, a messenger I am,
who, though far from you, greatly cares for and pities you.
sentences.i: I am a messenger of Zeus to you, who, though he is far from you, cares greatly for you and pities you.
sentences.n: Lines 26–27 again; only the final punctuation changes, an ano teleia for the full stop. For the forms see the first telling.

sentences.t:
θωρῆξαί σε κέλευσε κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιοὺς
πανσυδίῃ·
sentences.l:
to arm, he has bidden you, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
with-all-rush;
sentences.i: he has bidden you arm the long-haired Achaeans with all speed;
sentences.n: Lines 28–29 again. Agamemnon repeats the Dream’s second-person order to the elders as it was given to him.

sentences.t:
νῦν γάρ κεν ἕλοις πόλιν εὐρυάγυιαν
Τρώων·
sentences.l:
for now you might take the wide-streeted city
of the Trojans;
sentences.i: for now you could take the Trojans’ city of the wide streets;
sentences.n: Lines 29–30 again, with the ‘you’ of the Dream’s own words (ἕλοις), as Agamemnon heard them.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἀμφὶς Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες
ἀθάνατοι φράζονται·
sentences.l:
for no longer apart, who hold the Olympian halls,
the immortals plan;
sentences.i: for the immortals who hold the halls of Olympus no longer plan apart from one another;
sentences.n: The third time these words come in this part; here the Dream’s message about the gods is retold to the elders.

sentences.t:
ἐπέγναμψεν γὰρ ἅπαντας
Ἥρη λισσομένη, Τρώεσσι δὲ κήδε’ ἐφῆπται
ἐκ Διός·
sentences.i: for Hera, entreating them, has swayed them all, and sorrows have been fastened upon the Trojans from Zeus;
sentences.n: Lines 31–33 again, including the Dream’s addition ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’. What follows is shorter than the Dream’s own ending.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σὺ σῇσιν ἔχε φρεσίν·
sentences.l: but you, in your own wits hold it.’
sentences.i: but keep this in your own mind.’
sentences.n: The Dream’s speech ends here, with the first half of line 33 only (ἔχε φρεσίν, with final -ν where line 33 had φρεσί). Agamemnon’s version leaves out the warning against forgetfulness at 33–34. The single closing quotation mark ends the Dream’s speech; Agamemnon speaks on.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ μὲν εἰπὼν
ᾤχετ’ ἀποπτάμενος, ἐμὲ δὲ γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἀνῆκεν.
sentences.l:
So he, having spoken,
went off flying away, and me sweet sleep released.
sentences.i: With that he was gone, flying away, and sweet sleep let me go.
sentences.n: ὣς ὃ μὲν εἰπών: ὃ μέν ‘he’ (the Dream) contrasts with ἐμὲ δέ ‘but me’. ᾤχετ’ is ᾤχετο, the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘was gone’, with the aorist participle of ἀποπέτομαι ‘fly away’. ἀνῆκεν, aorist of ἀνίημι, is the verb of ἀνήῃ at line 34 (‘when sleep lets you go’). γλυκὺς ὕπνος is ‘sweet sleep’, a different Greek phrase from νήδυμος ὕπνος at 2.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ αἴ κέν πως θωρήξομεν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: But come, if in any way we might arm the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: But come, let us see if we can arm the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ ‘but come’, with ἄγετε the plural imperative. αἴ κέν πως is ‘if perhaps’, with θωρήξομεν, which can be read as a future indicative or as a short-vowel subjunctive of θωρήσσω ‘arm’: ‘let us see if we can’. υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός. The same line ends Nestor’s opening at 83, word for word.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα δ’ ἐγὼν ἔπεσιν πειρήσομαι, ἣ θέμις ἐστί,
καὶ φεύγειν σὺν νηυσὶ πολυκλήϊσι κελεύσω·
sentences.l:
and first I myself with words will make trial, as is the custom,
and bid them flee with their many-thwarted ships;
sentences.i: First I myself will make trial of them with words, as is the custom, and bid them flee with their ships of many thwarts;
sentences.n: πρῶτα … ἐγών: ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ. πειρήσομαι is ‘I will make trial’ (of the army, understood), with ἔπεσιν ‘with words’ the dative of means. ἣ θέμις ἐστί is ‘as is the custom’: ἥ is the relative, feminine like θέμις, ‘which is the custom’; θέμις is what established usage allows. φεύγειν σὺν νηυσί is ‘to flee with the ships’, that is, to sail home. νηυσί is the epic dative plural, and πολυκλήϊσι ‘of many thwarts’ (κληΐς, a rowing bench or thwart). Agamemnon tells the elders his plan before he tries it on the army.

sentences.t: ὑμεῖς δ’ ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος ἐρητύειν ἐπέεσσιν.
sentences.l: and you, from different sides, each one, hold them back with words.”
sentences.i: and you, each from a different quarter, must hold them back with words.”
sentences.n: ὑμεῖς δ’ ‘but you’ (plural) means the elders. ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is ‘one from one place, another from another’. ἐρητύειν is an infinitive standing for an imperative (as ἀγορευέμεν at 10), ‘hold back’, and ἐπέεσσιν the uncontracted dative plural of ἔπος, ‘with words’. The closing quotation mark ends Agamemnon’s speech.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὅ γ’ ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο, τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη
Νέστωρ, ὅς ῥα Πύλοιο ἄναξ ἦν ἠμαθόεντος,
sentences.l:
He then, having so spoken, sat down, and among them stood up
Nestor, who indeed was lord of sandy Pylos,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down, and among them there stood up Nestor, who was lord of sandy Pylos,
sentences.n: ἤτοι is printed as one word; ὅ γ’ is ‘he’ (Agamemnon), and κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο is the verb κατέζετο with its preposition apart (tmesis). τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη ‘and among them he stood up’. ἄναξ ‘lord’, with Πύλοιο the epic genitive. ἠμαθόεις ‘sandy’ (from ἄμαθος ‘sand’) is the stock epithet of Pylos. Agamemnon sits and Nestor rises: the formula marks a change of speaker.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: This line is the same as 1.73, where Calchas rises to speak. σφιν ‘to them’; ἐὺ φρονέων ‘thinking well’, that is kindly disposed; ἀγορήσατο ‘spoke in the assembly’, from ἀγοράομαι; μετέειπεν ‘spoke among them’. Nestor is introduced by a formula, and it prepares the reader for his speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
εἰ μέν τις τὸν ὄνειρον Ἀχαιῶν ἄλλος ἔνισπε
ψεῦδός κεν φαῖμεν καὶ νοσφιζοίμεθα μᾶλλον·
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives: if some other of the Achaeans had told of the dream, we should call it a falsehood and all the more turn away from it;
sentences.n: ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is ‘leaders and lords’, a stock address; here the army is Argives (79) and Achaeans (80) in two lines. εἰ μέν … ἔνισπε is ‘if … had told’ (ἔνισπε, aorist of ἐνέπω ‘tell’), τὸν ὄνειρον ‘the dream’ just heard. κεν with the optatives φαῖμεν ‘we should say’ and νοσφιζοίμεθα ‘we should turn away from’ (νοσφίζομαι) gives the answer. ψεῦδος is ‘a falsehood’.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἴδεν ὃς μέγ’ ἄριστος Ἀχαιῶν εὔχεται εἶναι·
sentences.l: but now he saw it, who by far the best of the Achaeans claims to be;
sentences.i: but as it is, he who claims to be by far the best of the Achaeans has seen it;
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ‘but as it is’ answers the supposition. ἴδεν is the unaugmented ἴδε(ν), ‘saw’ (Attic εἶδεν). ὃς μέγ’ ἄριστος Ἀχαιῶν εὔχεται εἶναι: μέγα with a superlative is ‘by far’, and εὔχεται εἶναι ‘claims to be’ (the verb that elsewhere means ‘pray’). Nestor points to Agamemnon without naming him.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ αἴ κέν πως θωρήξομεν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: But come, if in any way we might arm the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: But come, let us see if we can arm the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: This line is the same as 72, which closed Agamemnon’s plan; Nestor takes it up. Nestor’s speech runs on into the next part, so there is no closing quotation mark here.
